# Field Guide 02 | The debugging casebook

[← Architecture atlas](01_ARCHITECTURE_ATLAS.md) · [Volume II](../OMNIMASTER_FIELD_GUIDE.md) · [Next: Engineering workbook →](03_ENGINEERING_WORKBOOK.md)

A debugger's first obligation is to separate **what was observed** from **what might have caused it**. I want these cases to show my reasoning habits, not pretend that every diagnostic thought was a resolved production incident.

The cases below are derived from public PR reviews, engineering experiments and professional practice. The Fixer/CABO code-review cases identify actual open work; the manufacturing/analytics cases are **representative examples informed by past work**, not disclosures of protected client incidents.

## Case 01. A CDC loop can report success while making no progress

**Source:** [The Fixer PR #237](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/NewChanges/pull/237) and [CDC adapter issue #241](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/NewChanges/issues/241).  
**Evidence class:** Public code-review finding and an unresolved engineering task, not a completed production correction.

### Symptom

In the synthetic CDC runner, a batch limit is applied while accumulating row events. If a single row event exceeds the configured limit, the loop can stop rather than process the event. The run may still be recorded as a successful batch.

### Why I care

This is a subtle kind of failure: monitoring sees green, but the source checkpoint and destination state may stop progressing. A refreshed dashboard can look “live” while the underlying data remains stale.

### How I would diagnose it

1. Record the exact source event position and configured batch maximum.
2. Create a synthetic transaction whose row count is larger than that maximum.
3. Run the reader twice and compare checkpoint, processed-row count and job outcome.
4. Confirm whether the engine reports a retryable blocked state, progresses safely or silently repeats the same stalled position.
5. Check how checkpoint commit interacts with destination commit.

### Design alternatives

| Option | Benefit | Cost or risk |
|---|---|---|
| Fail closed on oversized event | Impossible to claim success while stalled | Requires operator response or controlled retry |
| Process oversized atomic event with explicit exception | Can preserve progress | Must respect transaction/memory limits |
| Split event carefully | Controls memory | Must preserve source transaction atomicity and ordering |

**My preferred invariant:** no successful CDC run without either real progress or an explicitly valid empty-source condition. The exact implementation needs transaction semantics reviewed in the target adapter.

**Proof needed before closure:** oversized-event regression, repeat polling, error status, retry and checkpoint consistency.

---

## Case 02. A year-end progression decision can target the wrong academic year

**Source:** [Learning Hub PR #160](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/Training-and-Development-Hub/pull/160) and [tracking issue #163](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/Training-and-Development-Hub/issues/163).  
**Evidence class:** Public cross-platform code-review finding. Still open until fixed and regression-tested.

### Symptom

An administrator loads learner progression candidates for academic year A, then changes the editable year control to B without forcing the candidates to refresh. A submission can use B to calculate the target year while still operating on candidate data that was reviewed for A.

### Why this matters

A UI state mismatch becomes a **data-integrity error** when submitted identifiers and derived fields have different temporal meaning.

### Investigation

- Trace where the year value lives in Android and iOS state.
- Trace the request parameter used to fetch candidates.
- Trace the value used for target-year derivation on submit.
- Change the year *after* a successful fetch and before confirmation.
- Verify whether the UI invalidates its selection or clearly binds it to the reviewed year.

### A stronger design

Treat each candidate set as a versioned decision context: **reviewed year + source request + selected records**. If the user changes the year, invalidate candidate state and require a refetch. On submit, bind the request to the reviewed context, and reject stale decisions server-side.

**Regression matrix:** Android, iOS, empty selection, year change, loading state, response ordering and server-side stale-context rejection.

---

## Case 03. The database snapshot is valid, but not a safe cutover

**Source:** [The Fixer guarded migration PR #225](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/NewChanges/pull/225) and the project's documented Aiven/Neon migration work.  
**Evidence class:** Historical test and migration-preparation record, not evidence of a completed live cutover.

### Symptom

A snapshot can have all expected tables and most correct row counts, while differences remain in an actively written audit table or in extension metadata. A schema restore passing does not mean the target is current enough for real traffic.

### Different questions that are often confused

**Schema parity:** Do tables, keys, functions, extensions, grants and migrations match?

**Data parity:** Is the target a consistent point-in-time representation of required source state?

**Security parity:** Can the application connect using restricted roles? Are there unintended privileges?

**Operational cutover readiness:** Can the old writer be fenced, final changes reconciled, and requests safely switched or rolled back?

### Investigation sequence

1. Capture a consistent source point and document any concurrent writes.
2. Compare schema, constraints, required functions and effective permissions.
3. Compare counts *and* checksums/key sets for required tables.
4. Investigate drift by table, especially append-only audit data.
5. Validate auth, MFA, tenant isolation and write functionality against a restricted target role.
6. Rehearse rollback and check which side is the sole authorised writer.

**My rule:** a successful restore proves the backup can be restored to some state. It does not prove zero data loss, current state, least privilege or a safe production switch.

---

## Case 04. “Email failed” can mean two different things

**Source:** [The Fixer security PR #233](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/NewChanges/pull/233).  
**Evidence class:** Source-remediation workstream and documented regression intent.

### Symptom

An outbound email is accepted by the transport, but persisting its audit record fails. Reporting the *whole operation* as a send failure can cause an operator to resend, producing an accidental duplicate.

### Hidden assumption

A single status field is being asked to represent two separate outcomes:

1. **Delivery request outcome:** what did the SMTP transport accept or reject?
2. **Audit persistence outcome:** did the platform save the record describing that action?

### Safer model

Represent outcomes independently, with a durable retry strategy for recording status rather than falsely telling the user the send did not happen. Where possible use idempotency keys and a transactional outbox to avoid dual-write inconsistencies.

### Tests I expect

- Transport accepts, audit succeeds.
- Transport rejects, audit attempts record the failure.
- Transport accepts, audit fails: UI does not falsely prompt resend.
- Retries do not duplicate a logically identical notification.
- Malformed addresses or header injections are denied before transport.

**Lesson:** when a workflow spans two independent systems, a single “success/fail” flag often hides the very distinction needed for safe recovery.

---

## Case 05. An apparently correct KPI can double-count industrial events

**Source context:** [Australian manufacturing and enterprise reporting case studies](../CLIENT_CASE_STUDIES.md).  
**Evidence class:** Illustrative teaching example based on the type of grain and join problems encountered in professional analytics. The fictional numbers below are not client records.

### Fictional sample

An order for **R1,000** has two dispatch rows and three quality-check rows. Joining order, dispatch and quality checks directly gives **six result rows**. Summing the order amount over those rows incorrectly yields **R6,000**.

### How I would isolate the problem

1. Establish the order table's primary grain as one row per order.
2. Check dispatch and inspection cardinalities independently.
3. Compare row counts before and after each join.
4. Choose whether to pre-aggregate child facts, model relationships or use separate fact tables.
5. Reconcile the expected R1,000 back to the source, both globally and under representative filters.
6. Measure performance **after** correctness is restored.

### Design decision

The fix is not an arbitrary DISTINCT or a visual-level filter that hides the problem. The model must reflect the business event being measured.

The accompanying [SQL Query Plans Lab](../../projects/sql-query-plans/) teaches index and predicate behaviour; it does not reproduce this specific grain example or any manufacturing data.

---

## Case 06. The best dashboard fix may be a database or API fix

**Source context:** [Engineering field notes](../ENGINEERING_FIELD_NOTES.md) and [professional client studies](../CLIENT_CASE_STUDIES.md).  
**Evidence class:** Representative diagnostic workflow.

If a page is slow, I divide the elapsed time into **source query, transformation, backend/API, browser/network and semantic calculation**. Each can fail independently.

| What I observe | Hypothesis | How I test |
|---|---|---|
| Raw query is slow | Scan, bad selectivity, missing index or costly joins | Query plan and comparable-row timing |
| Source SQL is fast but BI is slow | Model context, measure complexity or repeated transformations | Performance analyzer and controlled DAX/query comparisons |
| API slow under load | N+1 queries, missing indexes, connection pool pressure | Traces, query count, concurrency test |
| UI slow with fast API | Excess rendering, chart size, client-side transformations | Browser profiling and narrow-device tests |
| Results differ after optimisation | Semantic regression, duplicated joins or filter changes | Source reconciliation tests and snapshot comparison |

**Lesson:** instrument before redesigning. If a solution is faster but silently changes the intended figure, it failed the real test.

---

## The investigation template I use

~~~text
PROBLEM
User-visible impact:
Observed behaviour (with timestamp and environment):
What changed:
Expected invariant:

EVIDENCE
Reproducible steps:
Code/SQL/query plan:
Log/trace/test:
What is NOT known yet:

HYPOTHESES
1. ...
2. ...
3. ...

SAFE EXPERIMENTS
Disposable inputs:
Negative path:
Regression boundary:

DECISION
Smallest safe change:
Tests required:
Rollback strategy:
Residual risk:
Status: proposed / implemented / tested / deployed
~~~

The best incidents produce better contracts and tests, not just more alerts.

# Field Guide 03 | Engineering workbook

[← Debugging casebook](02_DEBUGGING_CASEBOOK.md) · [Volume II](../OMNIMASTER_FIELD_GUIDE.md) · [Next: Role and evidence map →](04_ROLE_AND_EVIDENCE_MAP.md)

This workbook turns the ideas in my profile into concrete problem-solving exercises. They are designed for engineering reviewers, interview panels and curious developers. **Inputs and sample numbers are fictional.** I include my reasoning, not hidden answer keys or claims that these exact questions came from interviews.

## How to use this chapter

Try each exercise before reading the discussion. Write down the business invariant, the failure mode, the smallest safe experiment and the evidence needed to consider the change done.

| Exercise | Skill | Estimated work |
|---|---|---|
| **A. The duplicate ledger amount** | Relational grain and BI semantics | Small SQL or paper exercise |
| **B. The missing CDC update** | Watermarks, ordering and replay | Design + code |
| **C. The unsafe bulk administrator endpoint** | RBAC, MFA and tenant isolation | API threat model |
| **D. The confident-but-unsupported AI answer** | Grounding, evaluation and human review | Python negative test |
| **E. The cutover that passed staging** | Release engineering and migrations | Deployment decision |
| **F. The query that got slower after indexing** | Query plans and selectivity | SQL profiling |
| **G. The incident briefing** | Technical communication | Two short explanations |

---

## Exercise A. The duplicate ledger amount

**Scenario:** An order table contains one invoice for 5,000 units of currency. The dispatch table contains two separate deliveries for that invoice. The QA table contains three inspection records. A report joins all three tables and sums invoice amounts.

**Questions**

1. What aggregate does the naive join produce?
2. Why is applying DISTINCT to the final invoice amount not a general solution?
3. What grain should each fact preserve?
4. How would you protect the fix against a new fourth QA record?

<details>
<summary>My worked reasoning</summary>

A direct two-child one-to-many join can produce 2 × 3 = **6 joined rows**, repeating the 5,000 invoice amount and reporting **30,000**. DISTINCT happens to hide some duplicates but breaks as soon as multiple legitimate invoices share the same value.

I would aggregate invoice value at invoice grain, model dispatch counts at delivery grain and QA counts at inspection grain, then relate them through stable identifiers and explicit dimensions. I would test the global amount, a filtered customer subtotal and a case with an extra QA row. The amount must remain 5,000.

A key requirement is that the invoice grain and its measure are defined **before** any join is optimised.

</details>

**Related history:** [Enterprise and manufacturing analytics](../CLIENT_CASE_STUDIES.md). **Runnable adjacent example:** [SQL query-plan lab](../../projects/sql-query-plans/).

## Exercise B. The missing CDC update

**Scenario:** The source stores an UPDATED_AT timestamp to second precision. Two updates to one account occur within that second. A loader advances its watermark to that timestamp and fetches rows with UPDATED_AT greater than the last value.

**Questions**

1. Which update can disappear from the consumer's history?
2. Will switching to greater-than-or-equal alone guarantee correctness?
3. How should DELETE operations be represented?
4. How do we make the checkpoint and destination transaction agree?

<details>
<summary>My worked reasoning</summary>

A strict greater-than predicate can skip writes sharing the last watermark. Greater-than-or-equal helps avoid missing a row but can replay rows, and it still cannot reconstruct two successive states or physical deletes from a final-state table.

I would first confirm the actual business requirement. For latest-state snapshots, a composite watermark such as timestamp plus stable key may work if the source exposes all needed changes and updates deterministically. For lossless event history and deletes, a genuine change log, transaction/binlog CDC or durable source event publishing is more suitable. I would combine an idempotent sink with a checkpoint that only advances after committed processing.

I would test two changes in one second, restart mid-batch, delete, out-of-order event and replay.

</details>

**Public reference:** [CDC Replay Lab](../../projects/cdc-replay-lab/) · [Fixer source-adapter issue](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/NewChanges/issues/241).

## Exercise C. The unsafe bulk administrator endpoint

**Scenario:** The React UI hides “bulk export” from ordinary employees. An employee discovers the API endpoint directly and submits a tenant ID belonging to another organisation.

**Questions**

1. Which checks must run on the server?
2. Is a logged-in session enough?
3. Where does MFA fit for sensitive actions?
4. How do you test denial without accidentally exposing other tenants' existence?

<details>
<summary>My worked reasoning</summary>

Front-end visibility is not authorisation. The API must authenticate the user, resolve their **authorised tenant scope from the server-side identity**, check operation permission and enforce data access constraints. Sensitive administrative actions may require current step-up proof and an auditable record.

I would test ordinary user requests, missing MFA, wrong role, cross-tenant parameters, revoked sessions, bulk pagination and alternate API paths. Negative responses must not return another tenant's rows, identifiers or counts. A database least-privileged role adds defense in depth; it does not replace a correct service permission model.

I would not call the control production-ready merely because a unit mock passes.

</details>

**Public reference:** [Fixer security workstream](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/NewChanges/pull/219) · [Security handbook](../handbook/07_SECURITY_AND_DELIVERY.md).

## Exercise D. The confident-but-unsupported AI answer

**Scenario:** A model is asked whether a fictional learning resource permits unlimited retakes. The approved document says **two retakes**, but the model answers “unlimited retakes” with a high claimed confidence.

**Questions**

1. Does a confidence score validate truth?
2. What evidence can an output validator compare?
3. Should a generated answer be allowed to update a learner's official grade?
4. What should happen when the provider is unavailable?

<details>
<summary>My worked reasoning</summary>

A high self-reported confidence score is not calibration. I would require an approved source identifier, source-grounded evidence, validated response shape and explicit handling for unknown or contradictory documents. An exact quotation validator can reject fabricated extracts, but does not establish that the source itself is correct or that a paraphrase is semantically faithful.

For grading or progression, I would use a controlled rubric, deterministic score limits, educator review, transparent correction and privacy-aware records. A provider failure should produce a safe fallback or an explicit **no-decision** state, not a fabricated grade.

The runnable demo intentionally restricts answers to extractive text because that is a verifiable toy contract.

</details>

**Run a negative test:** [Offline AI Output Evaluation](../../projects/ai-output-evaluation/). **Related product:** [CABO Learning Hub](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/Training-and-Development-Hub).

## Exercise E. The cutover that passed staging

**Scenario:** PostgreSQL schema restore and unit tests pass. The target contains a one-day-old snapshot, audit entries differ, and the source is still receiving live writes. The team wants to switch the primary app to the new database tonight.

**Questions**

1. Is a healthy connection a sufficient release gate?
2. What must happen to the old writer?
3. Which validation is missing?
4. What would make a rollback possible?

<details>
<summary>My worked reasoning</summary>

No. A connection proves reachability and perhaps permissions. It cannot prove data completeness, final replication, identity correctness, tenant security or cutover safety.

I would require a documented final-sync method, explicit old-writer fencing, data parity at a stable point, restricted-role privilege checks, application auth/MFA and write-path tests, backup/restore evidence, owner approval and a reversible rollout plan.

If those conditions cannot be met, the release should remain blocked. An attractive staging screenshot is not a substitute.

</details>

**Public reference:** [Guarded migration preparation](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/NewChanges/pull/225) · [Release principles](../handbook/07_SECURITY_AND_DELIVERY.md).

## Exercise F. The query that got slower after indexing

**Scenario:** A table stores tenant, status, date and amount. A developer adds a composite index on (tenant, status, date), but a dashboard query filters by a date-expression function and still performs slowly.

**Questions**

1. Which fields can the index still help?
2. What happens if the filter uses a direct inclusive/exclusive date range?
3. How can the test avoid confusing query correctness with performance?
4. Why might a database still choose a scan?

<details>
<summary>My worked reasoning</summary>

The equality prefix (tenant, status) may remain usable. Applying a function to the date column can prevent efficient use of the date range part. A direct predicate such as **date >= start and date < end** often gives the optimiser a better indexed range.

I would compare EXPLAIN output and verify identical aggregate results. On a real engine, I would also examine distribution, statistics, selectivity, table size, index maintenance and concurrency. The presence of an index does not require the optimiser to use it.

</details>

**Reproduce:** [SQL Query Plans Lab](../../projects/sql-query-plans/).

## Exercise G. Explain one issue twice

**Scenario:** A financial dashboard is missing updates because the underlying source timestamp cannot distinguish rapid consecutive changes.

Write two explanations:

- **For a technical reviewer:** describe timestamp precision, checkpoint/watermark risks, replay/deletion semantics and testing options.
- **For a business owner:** describe which numbers may be stale, how you will identify affected records and why the team should not present the dashboard as real time until checks are complete.

<details>
<summary>How I would communicate it</summary>

**Technical:** “The current incremental reader uses a second-resolution updated timestamp. Multiple events can share the checkpoint value, and a strict greater-than query may miss them. It also does not represent physical deletes. We need a verified source-change mechanism or a bounded reconciliation strategy with duplicate-safe replay. I'll prove this with a synthetic multiple-write test before changing the reporting freshness claim.”

**Business:** “Some changes made close together may not be reflected in the dashboard. We're testing the source and comparing it with the displayed records. Until the gap is fixed and measured, the figures should be treated as periodically updated rather than live.”

</details>

## A reviewer can use this rubric

| Criterion | Weak answer | Strong answer |
|---|---|---|
| **Business understanding** | Lists technologies | Defines the real event, audience and decision |
| **Data correctness** | Assumes joins are safe | States grain, keys and reconciliation invariants |
| **Failure handling** | “Retry until it works” | Covers idempotency, ordering, limits and rollback |
| **Security** | Hides controls in the UI | Enforces role, tenant and purpose server-side |
| **AI quality** | Trusts model confidence | Grounds evidence, validates output, requires human control |
| **Testing** | Reports “tests pass” | Names exact cases, commit, environment and missing proof |
| **Communication** | Hides uncertainty | States what is known, unknown and safe to release |

The aim is not to memorise these answers. It's to make the assumptions visible enough that a colleague can challenge them.

[← Engineering workbook](03_ENGINEERING_WORKBOOK.md) · [Volume II](../OMNIMASTER_FIELD_GUIDE.md) · [Next: Decision journal →](05_DECISION_JOURNAL.md)

**Who I am:** Cayelaem Jantjies, a Johannesburg-based data engineer, analytics engineer and full-stack developer with a BCom in Statistics and Data Science from the University of Pretoria (2023) and over three years of professional experience.

**My specialisation is connected delivery:** tracing a business problem through source data, transformations, semantic models, APIs, applications, access control, testing and operations.

|---|---|---|
| Banking dashboards spanning **four African markets** | Multi-market analytics, security-aware measures, commercial reporting | [Professional banking case](../CLIENT_CASE_STUDIES.md) |
| Commercial research involving **270M+ survey records** | Large reporting scope, model grain, data preparation and performance focus | [FMCG research case](../CLIENT_CASE_STUDIES.md) |

## Find the relevant engineering perspective

### If you are hiring a Data Engineer or Data Platform Engineer

**My relevant work:** SQL Server/T-SQL, SQL staging, ELT/ETL design, dataflow failures, Microsoft Fabric exposure, operational source integration, PostgreSQL/MySQL modelling and source freshness investigations.

**Examples to review:** [Australian manufacturing](../handbook/03_SYSTEMS_IN_THE_WILD.md) · [Data engineering chapter](../handbook/04_DATA_ENGINEERING.md) · [CDC lab](../../projects/cdc-replay-lab/) · [CDC issue #241](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/NewChanges/issues/241).

**What I would discuss:** late-arriving facts, restart-safe ingestion, watermark collisions, model grain, index selection, data contracts, recovery and measurable freshness.

**Growth edge:** deeper real-time/distributed stream operations and platform-scale orchestration; I do not equate a synthetic lab with a production Kafka/Flink deployment.

### If you are hiring an Analytics Engineer or BI Engineer

**My relevant work:** Power BI, DAX, Power Query M, SQL, dimensional modelling, multi-market security/reporting, manufacturing/financial metrics and optimisation.

**Examples to review:** [Case studies](../CLIENT_CASE_STUDIES.md) · [BI chapter](../handbook/05_ANALYTICS_ENGINEERING.md) · [SQL query-plan lab](../../projects/sql-query-plans/).

**What I would discuss:** semantic ownership, star schemas, RLS, time intelligence, repeatable KPIs, the effect of query shape and business interpretation.

**Growth edge:** scaling governance and observability across larger enterprise semantic-model estates and new Fabric workloads.

### If you are hiring a Full-Stack or Backend Engineer

**My relevant work:** React, TypeScript, Fastify/Node.js, PostgreSQL/Prisma, APIs, integrations, admin workflows, validation, testing and cloud delivery considerations.

**Examples to review:** [The Fixer](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/NewChanges) · [End-to-end system atlas](01_ARCHITECTURE_ATLAS.md) · [Release and security chapter](../handbook/07_SECURITY_AND_DELIVERY.md).

**What I would discuss:** service boundaries, role and tenant security, schema changes, retries, idempotency, API negative cases, testing and deployment rollback.

**Growth edge:** bigger multi-team service ownership, incident response at scale and longer-running operational reliability programs.

### If you are hiring for Applied AI / AI Product Engineering

**My relevant work:** integrating task-based AI capabilities into learning/product workflows, evidence-aware outputs, provider-routing experiments, fallback behaviour and human approval boundaries.

**Examples to review:** [Learning Hub](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/Training-and-Development-Hub) · [AI product chapter](../handbook/06_PRODUCTS_AND_AI.md) · [Offline AI evaluation lab](../../projects/ai-output-evaluation/).

**What I would discuss:** output contracts, evaluation sets, source provenance, PII constraints, provider errors, latency/cost and how to keep consequential decisions reviewable.

**Growth edge:** production-grade benchmark design, monitoring/calibration and cross-provider security operations. Model integration is not a claim of training or running proprietary foundation models.

### If you are assessing a Solution Architect / Technical Leadership pathway

**My relevant work:** bridging commercial/operational requirements with SQL, application design, access rules, integration/testing and release risk. Independent product development has expanded my understanding of trade-offs across functions.

**Examples to review:** [Leadership chapter](../handbook/09_LEADERSHIP_AND_NEXT.md) · [Architecture atlas](01_ARCHITECTURE_ATLAS.md) · [Decision journal](05_DECISION_JOURNAL.md).

**What I would discuss:** business outcomes, scope boundaries, compliance, budget, architecture fitness, staged release gates and technical documentation.

**Growth edge:** formal technical leadership and larger-team architectural accountability. **This is a career direction, not a claim that I currently hold a CTO title.**

| **Data / BI** | SQL Server, Power BI, DAX, Power Query, Fabric, ETL/ELT, dimensional modelling | Depth varies by engagement and tool |
| **Backend** | TypeScript, Node.js/Fastify, REST APIs, PostgreSQL, MySQL/SQL Server integrations | Product work includes active/staging PRs |
| **Frontend** | React, TypeScript, web UX, dashboard/chart interfaces | Not all independent frontends have full feature parity |

| **Cloud** | Render, Cloudflare, AWS RDS experiments, Aiven/Neon migration preparation | Cutover candidates have independent gating and cost constraints |

The [complete skills matrix](../TECHNICAL_SKILLS.md) provides more specific caveats.

## What I'd like a reviewer to challenge me on

- Where would I store a source event so recovery stays possible?
- How do I distinguish a correct-looking dashboard from a correct metric?
- When would I place transformation in the database instead of the application?
- How would I design administrative MFA recovery without introducing a bypass?
- What evidence would persuade me *not* to release?
- How does applied AI create real product value while respecting people and their data?

These are useful conversations because the answers require concrete engineering judgment.

# Field Guide 05 | Architecture decision journal

[← Role and evidence map](04_ROLE_AND_EVIDENCE_MAP.md) · [Volume II](../OMNIMASTER_FIELD_GUIDE.md) · [Main handbook](../OMNIMASTER_HANDBOOK.md)

The choice of technology matters less than the reasoning and trade-offs behind it. I like to keep decisions inspectable: **context, options, decision, risks, verification and revisit triggers**.

These are teaching-oriented decision records reflecting questions in my work. They are not a complete history of formal company approvals or claims that each option was deployed.

## ADR-01 | Where should data transformation happen?

**Status:** Context-dependent design principle, not a blanket implementation.

**Problem:** An application ingests data from SQL, API and file sources. Repeatedly moving whole datasets into an application database to perform report-only calculations increases latency, duplication and reconciliation burden.

### Options

| Option | Strength | Weakness |
|---|---|---|
| All transformations in app code | Flexible domain rules and common programming tooling | May duplicate large datasets and bypass database optimisation |
| Push all rules to source SQL | Less data transfer and efficient set-based processing | Couples business logic to source schema and database permissions |
| Hybrid source projection + curated semantics | Can keep heavy filtering/joins near data while preserving app policy | Needs explicit ownership and consistent contract versioning |

**My preferred approach:** place large, set-based, source-specific calculations where the engine can do them safely; keep cross-source policy, access decisions and application transactions in the appropriate service boundary. Define the data contract once and validate the highest-risk invariants, rather than multiplying inconsistent checks.

**How I test the decision:** compare plans, data movement, transformation ownership, result reconciliation, security scope and end-to-end freshness on a disposable environment.

**Revisit if:** source systems cannot support required indexes/privileges; business rules change frequently; multiple consumers need a shared versioned curated layer.

**Related:** [Data architecture atlas](01_ARCHITECTURE_ATLAS.md) · [The Fixer](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/NewChanges).

---

## ADR-02 | How do we capture source changes?

**Status:** A real design question under investigation; no completed production CDC claim.

**Problem:** A polling approach can miss timestamp collisions and physical deletes. A binlog reader introduces privileges, transaction semantics and operational overhead.

**Options:** stable incremental queries plus reconciliation, transaction/binlog CDC, source event publishing or periodic full snapshots.

**Decision criterion:** the **actual freshness and completeness contract**, not the marketing phrase “real time.”

If the business can tolerate scheduled reporting and a reliable source version is available, simpler incremental extraction may be right. If every mutation and delete must be represented, CDC/event logs become more compelling.

**Verification:** same-second updates, deletes, restart at the checkpoint boundary, oversized event handling, retention expiry, duplicate delivery, source snapshot consistency and measured consumer lag.

**Public work:** [CDC source adapter issue #241](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/NewChanges/issues/241) · [CDC educational lab](../../projects/cdc-replay-lab/).

---

## ADR-03 | How should we move a live application between database providers?

**Status:** Release principle drawn from guarded Neon/Aiven work. A migration candidate is not a completed switch.

**Problem:** Backups, application identity, active writers and audit data must agree at cutover. Schema parity alone is insufficient.

**Options considered:** in-place upgrade, offline snapshot copy, managed replication/CDC or a timed maintenance-window switch.

**Preferred policy:** no live switch until there is a verified final source state, final sync, writer fencing, least-privileged credentials, tested auth/MFA, complete required data reconciliation, an approved traffic plan and a recovery route. Do not let a cost-saving target or a green migration script waive these gates.

**Verification:** restore test, extension/function/privilege review, source-target parity, single-writer invariant, application smoke tests, rollback rehearsal and explicit sign-off.

**Revisit if:** the application supports online dual-read/single-writer migration, the outage tolerance changes or the provider's runtime/connection limits differ materially.

**Related:** [Migration PR #225](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/NewChanges/pull/225) · [Debugging casebook](02_DEBUGGING_CASEBOOK.md).

---

## ADR-04 | How should privileged actions prove identity?

**Status:** Active security design, not an unconditional production guarantee.

**Problem:** An administrator can possess a valid login session without having recently proved control of a strong authentication factor. Enrolment and recovery are frequent bypass risks.

**Options:** password-only, session-wide TOTP, WebAuthn/passkeys with step-up and controlled recovery, or externally managed identity with equivalent enforced claims.

**Preferred policy:** server-enforced role and tenant checks for every privileged operation; fresh strong MFA evidence for high-risk actions; no first-time-enrolment bypass granting general admin access; replay-resistant recovery and auditability.

**Verification:** route enumeration, direct HTTP negative requests, ordinary-user denial, session revocation, TOTP replay prevention, passkey origin binding, recovery separation and production secret configuration.

**Revisit if:** federated enterprise identity becomes authoritative or legal/operational requirements change.

**Related:** [Fixer admin MFA PR #219](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/NewChanges/pull/219) · [Security chapter](../handbook/07_SECURITY_AND_DELIVERY.md).

---

## ADR-05 | What role should AI have in consequential workflows?

**Status:** Applied-AI product design direction with selected code experiments, not independent certification.

**Problem:** A model can be helpful at drafting, explaining and evaluating source-bound responses, but it may fabricate evidence, expose data or give inconsistent advice.

**Options:** unconditional autonomous decisions, no AI at all, or bounded AI assistance with source provenance and human oversight.

**Preferred policy:** use AI where it makes a specific workflow more useful and where there is a deterministic boundary for identity, permission, output structure and irreversible changes. Human review is required for consequential learner, candidate and finance decisions.

**Verification:** source-grounded evaluation sets, refusal/unknown handling, tenant isolation, prompt-injection attacks, output schema checks, latency/cost budgets, failover, fairness review and appeals.

**Revisit if:** assessment requirements, provider costs, model reliability, regulations or allowed data flows change.

**Related:** [Learning Hub](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/Training-and-Development-Hub) · [Offline AI evaluation lab](../../projects/ai-output-evaluation/).

---

## ADR-06 | What should a “green” CI status actually mean?

**Status:** Engineering release philosophy and an implemented test boundary in this profile.

**Problem:** A workflow can complete successfully even when it did not test the real deployment surface, the latest commit or the relevant negative paths.

**Preferred policy:** make each status precise. **Green lab CI** means the local synthetic labs and documentation checks passed at the commit under test. **Green release gate** would require the applicable application, browser, database, security, migration and operational validation on the intended release artifact.

A documentation change should not assert a Fixer MFA release merely because the profile's Python tests passed.

**Evidence:** [Profile CI workflow](../../.github/workflows/engineering-labs-ci.yml). It tests four self-contained labs and the handbook's local navigation, not The Fixer's live infrastructure.

**Revisit if:** a project adds more consumers, secrets, external integrations, supported runtimes or new legal/release requirements.

---

## The decision-record template I use

~~~text
Decision:
Status: proposed / accepted / implemented / verified / superseded
Date and context:
Owner and reviewers:

Problem and invariant:
Requirements:
Constraints (security, cost, compliance, latency, skills):
Options considered:
Chosen option and why:
Rejected options and why:

Known risks:
Operational impact:
How we will test:
Evidence required for release:
Rollback:
Revisit conditions:
References:
~~~

## My broader view

Choosing the newest platform is easy. Choosing a platform whose costs, failure modes, governance and maintenance fit the problem is more demanding. That's the practice I want to deepen as I grow toward solution architecture and technical leadership.

# Personal Chapter 01 | INTJ and me

[← Operating manual](../OMNIMASTER_OPERATING_MANUAL.md) · [Next →](02_WHY_I_THINK_IN_SYSTEMS.md)

## The name I use for my default mode

I identify with the **INTJ** description. In everyday language, I see myself as strategic, analytical, independent, private when I am thinking, and interested in what a system could become rather than only what it is today.

That description is a useful *personal shorthand*. Myers-Briggs types are not a precise scientific explanation for personality, intelligence, work performance or career fit. I do not use the label to evaluate other people or justify behaviour.

What matters is the specific set of habits I can explain and improve.

## How those habits appear in my engineering

| Tendency I recognise | Helpful side | Risk I have to watch |
|---|---|---|
| I ask “why does this work?” repeatedly | I trace incorrect data through several system layers | I can over-investigate when a smaller safe fix is enough |
| I plan several steps ahead | I anticipate migration, security and operational constraints | I may spend too long designing future capabilities |
| I like independent ownership | I can move from SQL to backend, tests and UI without constant handoffs | I must communicate progress instead of disappearing into the work |
| I challenge assumptions | I notice missing keys, vague KPIs and false claims of readiness | Questions can sound sharper than intended |
| I learn by building | I convert concepts into runnable examples and product experiments | Side projects can multiply before the earlier ones are polished |
| I prefer direct feedback | Problems get surfaced before they become expensive | I should adapt delivery to the person's context |

The point is not to romanticise any personality type. The point is to be accountable for how my preferences affect the team.

## Introversion does not mean avoiding collaboration

I value uninterrupted time for difficult problems. I also know that the people closest to a business workflow often understand constraints that a codebase cannot reveal.

I want a teammate to feel comfortable saying, “Your model is elegant, but it doesn't match the process.” That's useful feedback.

My preferred loop is **listen to the real workflow → inspect the data → test the hypothesis → share the result → adjust together**.

## How I make decisions

I usually want the invariant before the implementation. For a CDC problem, I ask what changes must never be lost. For an admin feature, I ask who must never be allowed to execute it. For an AI assessment, I ask which output cannot be accepted automatically.

A project discussion goes better when everyone knows the actual constraint:

- **Business:** what changes for the person using the result?
- **Data:** who owns the source truth?
- **Security:** what must never be exposed or changed?
- **Operations:** what happens when a service fails or money runs out?
- **Evidence:** what test proves the intended behaviour?

## What I'm still learning about myself

I can be tempted to chase completeness, build everything and take personal responsibility for every layer. There is an upside: I know where systems meet. The downside: a team needs focused scope, clear handoffs and room for other people to own expert decisions.

So I practise separating **must ship**, **must prove before release** and **interesting later**.

## My relationship with curiosity

Sometimes I want to see how a thing works purely because it exists. I will test a SQL assumption in SQLite, create a synthetic pipeline, investigate the API behind a user interface, or ask whether an AI feature has any business value after you include evaluation costs.

That is not an INTJ superpower. It is a learning habit I have deliberately reinforced through work.

## A note to anyone reading this

You do not need to be INTJ to work like me, and being INTJ does not make someone technically capable. The habits worth copying are **critical thinking, independent verification, clear communication, thoughtful planning and learning in public without disclosing private data**.

For practical examples, see the [OmniMaster Academy](../OMNIMASTER_ACADEMY.md) and [engineering investigations](../field-guide/02_DEBUGGING_CASEBOOK.md).

# Personal Chapter 02 | Why I think in systems

[← INTJ and me](01_INTJ_AND_ME.md) · [Operating manual](../OMNIMASTER_OPERATING_MANUAL.md) · [Next →](03_IT_RANGE_AND_LIMITS.md)

## My professional curiosity has an origin

I studied **Statistics and Data Science at the University of Pretoria**, graduating with a BCom in 2023. That made me interested in what evidence can actually support. Later, professional BI work taught me that numbers become dangerous when they look authoritative but were modelled carelessly.

And the more operational systems I worked with, the more I learned that a report is only one surface of a larger machine.

## The journey that changed my questions

### First: make the analysis correct

In reporting work I cared about cleaning data, matching sources, writing useful DAX/SQL, and making results intelligible to business users.

That taught me that even a simple question like “how many?” depends on populations, relationships, dates and exclusions.

### Then: make the pipeline repeatable

When reports depend on manual exports, shifting schemas and complex operational source queries, the workflow becomes the real engineering problem.

Automation pushed my thinking toward staging, source contracts, retries, scheduler behaviour, transformations, monitoring and data governance.

### Then: make the application usable

A dashboard can explain a problem, but people may need to act on it. That draws in React, APIs, PostgreSQL, identity, admin tools, validation, transactions and interfaces.

I started thinking less about a single output and more about a full path from **user intent to an authorised, durable state change**.

### Then: make the system safe to operate

Security and infrastructure work exposed the uncomfortable part of building things: a branch can pass tests and still be unsafe to release. Credentials, MFA enrolment, tenant isolation, source access, database parity and rollback are not optional chapters in a real product.

### Now: ask whether intelligence improves anything

Applied AI interests me because it can assist with difficult tasks, especially learning, reporting and workflow analysis. But my instinct remains the same: where is the source evidence, what is deterministic, who reviews, and how does failure behave?

## What connects the industries

I have worked across banking, manufacturing, FMCG, media, agriculture and social impact. They have different terminology and users, but many recurring technical problems:

- A source record means something different from how a downstream user reads it.
- Two legitimate events are accidentally counted as one or one event is counted twice.
- Permissions are applied to a screen but not enforced on the backend.
- A complex process is repeated manually because the systems do not integrate.
- A confident-looking output hides uncertainty or stale data.
- An implementation is considered complete before its failure path has been tested.

These patterns made me increasingly curious about the **connections between disciplines**.

## One example of how I work

Imagine an operations dashboard has a wrong total.

**Shortcut:** alter the DAX formula until the visual matches an expected number.

**My preferred route:**

1. Define the business quantity and time period.
2. Reconcile raw source records and grain.
3. Check transformations and keys.
4. Inspect the semantic model and security filters.
5. Profile the query if latency is involved.
6. Fix the smallest layer that owns the error.
7. Add a regression test and explain the change to the business.

That method scales from a report to a platform.

## Why I build independent products

Client work gives me real constraints, stakeholders and delivery pressure. Independent projects let me explore how those disciplines meet across an entire product lifecycle, including architecture, onboarding, pricing ideas, privacy, user experience, tests and infrastructure.

That is why my portfolio spans learning systems, finance software, workforce tooling, data integration, commerce experiments and tiny synthetic labs. Not everything is released; the point is to learn the hard parts honestly.

## The contradiction I live with

I enjoy breadth. Engineering expertise also requires depth and restraint. Being able to move between topics is useful only when I know **when a specialist is needed**, what evidence is missing, and what not to claim.

That tension is part of why I am working toward solution architecture and technical leadership while remaining hands-on.

## A habit you can copy today

For your next bug, keep a tiny journal:

~~~text
What I saw:
What I assumed:
What the source really showed:
My smallest experiment:
The actual cause:
What I changed:
What would prove the fix:
What I still do not know:
~~~

Over time, this record explains how you think much more convincingly than a list of tools.

[Professional case studies](../CLIENT_CASE_STUDIES.md) · [Why my range matters](03_IT_RANGE_AND_LIMITS.md) · [Learn the workflow](../OMNIMASTER_ACADEMY.md).

# Personal Chapter 03 | Where I fit across IT

[← Why I think in systems](02_WHY_I_THINK_IN_SYSTEMS.md) · [Operating manual](../OMNIMASTER_OPERATING_MANUAL.md) · [Next →](04_COLLABORATION_AND_QUIRKS.md)

## My short answer

**Put me in almost any software-facing IT environment, give me a real problem, access to the relevant system and time to understand the domain, and I can usually find a useful contribution.**

**Hardware engineering, physical electronics and device repair are not my specialisation.** I'm not saying I could never learn them, just that my demonstrated work is overwhelmingly in data and software systems.

The distinction matters: **broad problem-solving ability is not the same as already being fully qualified for every specialist role**. I wouldn't claim that because I can build APIs I am automatically a specialist kernel engineer, a certified penetration tester or a senior network architect.

## My capability landscape

| Discipline | How I fit | Evidence | Honest boundary |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Data Engineering** | **Core hands-on strength** | SQL, staging, transformations, manufacturing, source contracts, [CDC lab](../../projects/cdc-replay-lab/) | Deep distributed streaming and scale-specific operations need project evidence |
| **Analytics / BI** | **Core hands-on strength** | Power BI, DAX, Fabric-related work, enterprise modelling and [professional case studies](../CLIENT_CASE_STUDIES.md) | New vendor-specific certifications not claimed |
| **Full-Stack / Backend** | **Hands-on application delivery** | React, TypeScript, Node.js/Fastify, REST, PostgreSQL, [The Fixer](https://github.com/CayelaemJ/NewChanges) | Some product features remain drafts or staging |
| **Database Engineering** | **Practical design and operations** | SQL Server, PostgreSQL, MySQL, schema validation, SQL performance and migration preparation | Not a claim to be a dedicated DBA across every engine |
| **Cloud / DevOps / Platform** | **Active hands-on growth** | Render, Cloudflare, AWS RDS experimentation, CI, Docker, staged migrations | Production SRE/on-call and advanced cloud operations need separate proof |
| **Security Engineering** | **Security-conscious development** | MFA, authz, threat-aware reviews, scanner triage, negative tests and gated PRs | Not a specialist red-team or incident-forensics credential |
| **Applied AI / ML Products** | **Product integration and responsible evaluation** | Learning workflow experiments, provider routing, [evaluation lab](../../projects/ai-output-evaluation/) | Not claiming foundation-model research or verified production training infrastructure |
| **Mobile / Native** | **Developing engineering capability** | Kotlin/Android and iOS workstreams, cross-platform design | Full native parity and device validation are works in progress |
| **Business Analysis / Product Engineering** | **Strong problem-to-system translation** | KPI definitions, stakeholder delivery, prototypes and operational workflows | Formal product executive leadership is a future path |
| **Quality / Automation** | **Hands-on testing and CI** | Python unit tests, Docker workflows, Playwright/Vitest work and [profile CI](../../.github/workflows/engineering-labs-ci.yml) | Test coverage is project-specific, not universal |
| **Networking / Infrastructure / Systems Administration** | **Able to collaborate and learn** | Application connectivity, access and deployment troubleshooting | Specialist network operations and low-level systems roles require focused learning |
| **Hardware / Electronics / Physical IT** | **Not my focus** | No claim of circuit design, hardware repair or physical infrastructure engineering | Would require an entirely different training and evidence path |

## Why breadth has practical value

When a reporting issue appears, it might live in SQL, a dataflow, an API, access controls, a DAX calculation or a browser interaction. Somebody who can investigate more than one layer can narrow the fault before escalating.

When a new product is designed, the same cross-stack view helps identify ownership and integration risks early: where an event originates, who can mutate it, how a user sees it, and what happens when a dependency fails.

I have been the person working across those boundaries in professional and independent projects.

## Where breadth can become a weakness

I do not want to use versatility as an excuse to be vague or skip depth. Specialist systems deserve specialist review. My contribution can be to understand the interface, diagnose the problem, design the integration or help coordinate a safe solution, without pretending I have personally run every class of infrastructure.

**The strongest version of my career story is not “I know everything”. It is “I know how to learn, investigate, connect systems and deliver across several important engineering domains.”**

## A practical interview answer

> I am strongest in data engineering, analytics engineering and full-stack software delivery, with hands-on experience stretching into applied AI, security-minded development, cloud and DevOps. I've worked through source data, databases, APIs, interfaces, testing and deployments rather than only one layer. That makes me adaptable across most software-oriented IT teams. I'm not positioning myself as a hardware engineer or an instant expert in every specialist niche. I bring a strong foundation, practical problem-solving and the discipline to close the skill gaps a role requires.

## Where I'm going

I want to grow toward solutions architecture and technology leadership because I enjoy the responsibilities between disciplines: business value, system design, risk, cost, team coordination and long-term reliability.

**Breadth gets me into the conversation. Evidence and sound judgment keep me there.**

# Personal Chapter 04 | How to work with me (and a few quirks)

[← My range across IT](03_IT_RANGE_AND_LIMITS.md) · [Operating manual](../OMNIMASTER_OPERATING_MANUAL.md) · [Enter the arcade →](../OMNIMASTER_ARCADE.md)

I want my work to be serious. I don't need the GitHub to be solemn.

## A collaborator's cheat sheet

| If you want to… | The best way to work with me |
|---|---|
| **Describe a business problem** | Tell me who is affected, what the current result is and what correct would look like |
| **Report a bug** | Include an example, expected/actual outcome and the environment; a screenshot can help but source data semantics matter more |
| **Suggest an architecture** | Explain the constraints and why the trade-off is worthwhile; I don't need every answer to use my favourite stack |
| **Review my work** | Challenge assumptions and failure cases directly; specific feedback is useful |
| **Give me autonomy** | Agree on the outcome, guardrails and decision points; then let me investigate and show evidence |
| **Ask for an update** | I should distinguish done, tested, staging, blocked and proposed, with links to evidence |
| **Disagree with me** | Show the counterexample; if the evidence changes, the design should change |

## My default thinking pattern

**Problem → source → constraints → model → implementation → tests → release evidence.**

If I sound overly interested in the source table for a UI bug, it's probably because I have seen a clean interface present incorrect information before.

## Things I enjoy

I like engineering puzzles that require a little detective work. I enjoy taking a vague business request and making the invisible system visible. I like the point where a query plan, data model, API contract and UI all tell the same story. And I enjoy building things independently, not only to ship products but to test ideas that cross disciplines.

Some of that shows up in my OmniMaster persona. The superhero theme is playful. The desire to connect systems, learn deeply and solve real problems is sincere.

## A tiny personality stress test

<details>
<summary>Someone says: “We only need a simple dashboard.”</summary>

My first thoughts: What is the business grain? Where does the data come from? What is the access boundary? Is the refresh promise accurate? Are we about to spend two months on a problem that needs one good SQL query?

Then I remember the useful skill is not listing every possible failure. It is asking the **few questions that change the design**.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Someone says: “The CI passed so production is ready.”</summary>

I would ask what CI actually tested and on which commit. Unit tests, integration checks, migration rehearsal, real privileges and rollback all prove different things. “Green” is a claim with a scope.

</details>

<details>
<summary>Someone says: “Let's add AI to everything.”</summary>

I'd start with the user problem. If deterministic software solves it, use that. If AI meaningfully helps, define the source evidence, permitted data, output contract, evaluation and human control. A model call shouldn't become a product requirement by accident.

</details>

## The part I actively work on

I enjoy independence and control over a complete problem. That can become a trap if I take on too much, overengineer a solution or communicate after the fact. The improvement is practical: smaller milestones, documented decision points, early feedback, clear ownership and the humility to ask a specialist.

I want to be the person who can diagnose across layers **and** bring other people into the work.

## A personal code of conduct

- No pretending a prototype is a shipped product.
- No exposing client records to prove my ability.
- No demeaning the person who spotted a bug.
- No confusing a clever technical answer with a useful one.
- No hiding uncertainty behind a personality label.
- No treating the hardware team as somehow less technical because their expertise is different.
- Keep the fun. Real engineering has enough incident reports already.

## The unofficial scorecard

| Attribute | What I aspire to |
|---|---|
| Curiosity | High enough to ask a second question |
| Rigour | High enough to test the first answer |
| Adaptability | High enough to change the design |
| Communication | Clear enough that someone else can use it |
| Humility | High enough to say “I don't know yet” |
| Playfulness | Enough to make the repository enjoyable |

## What is an OmniMaster?

Not somebody who is magically certified in every technology. An OmniMaster is the character I use to express an engineering ambition: **understand enough of every connected layer to make the whole system better**, while respecting the specialists and people who make it possible.

And yes, it is perfectly reasonable to have a technical autobiography with an arcade. If a repository can contain a YAML file that controls a release, it can survive a small personality.

[Visit the OmniMaster Arcade](../OMNIMASTER_ARCADE.md) · [Study in the Academy](../OMNIMASTER_ACADEMY.md) · [Back to the operating manual](../OMNIMASTER_OPERATING_MANUAL.md)
